canonical_statement: The ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes contains current clinical practice recommendations and is updated annually or more frequently as warranted by the ADA Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes.
This section directs readers to the separate Introduction and Methodology for the detailed evidence-grading system and full Professional Practice Committee information.

Treatment decisions should be timely, rely on evidence-based guidelines, address social determinants of health, and incorporate shared decision-making based on individual values, preferences, prognosis, comorbidities, and informed financial considerations.

Diabetes management should align with evidence-based care models emphasizing person-centered team care, integrated long-term treatment of diabetes and comorbidities, and ongoing collaborative communication and goal setting.

Care systems should facilitate in-person and virtual team-based care, include team members experienced in diabetes management, and use patient registries, decision support, proactive care planning, and community involvement.
Diabetes management, risk factors, and complications should be assessed with reliable and relevant data metrics while considering individual values, goals, treatment burden, and costs.
Health systems should adopt continuous quality improvement, benchmarking, and interprofessional teams to support sustainable and scalable process changes that improve care and outcomes.

Health systems should assess and address gaps in diabetes care and outcomes by stratifying clinical quality data by factors such as insurance status, race, ethnicity, preferred language, disability, and social determinants of health.

Clinical encounters should assess social determinants of health, including food insecurity, housing insecurity, financial barriers, insurance and care access, environmental and neighborhood factors, and social/community support, to inform treatment decisions and referrals.

canonical_statement: The section states that approximately 9 in 10 American adults are estimated to have limited or low health literacy.
The section describes health literacy and numeracy as important to diabetes prevention and management and recommends reducing unnecessary complexity when developing care plans.
Telehealth should complement rather than replace in-person visits for optimal glycemic management.

Reported telehealth successes in marginalized populations often depend on infrastructure and targeted digital-literacy or community-health-worker support that are rarely part of routine care; without this support, attrition is high.
The section identifies financial, informational, and technical barriers as drivers of the digital divide and warns that inaccessible telehealth design can exacerbate existing inequities.

Inconsistent findings across Chronic Care Model components may reflect heterogeneity of interventions, settings, evaluation strategies, structural barriers to program use, and differing community needs.

Table 1.1 recommends the following team-care approach for all adults with diabetes: Engage primary care, diabetes care and education, nutrition, and other appropriate specialists; assess and address social determinants of health.

Table 1.1 recommends the following team-care approach for adults treated with intensive insulin therapy: Engage clinicians and team members experienced in advanced diabetes management, including diabetes technology use.

source_anchor.table_row: Adults treated with intensive insulin therapy

canonical_statement: Table 1.1 recommends the following team-care approach for children and adolescents with diabetes: Use an interprofessional pediatric team with school/daycare and caregiver involvement; address SDOH, safety, well-being, academic performance, school diabetes planning, and developmentally appropriate transfer of self-management.

Table 1.1 recommends the following team-care approach for people with diabetes-related complications or comorbidities: Use appropriate specialty referrals, care coordination, and clinical pharmacist involvement for polypharmacy or complex medication plans; screen for barriers and self-care demand exceeding capacity/resources.

source_anchor.table_row: People with diabetes-related complications or comorbidities

canonical_statement: Table 1.1 recommends the following team-care approach for people with social and/or structural barriers to care: Engage care navigation, social services, insurance support, peer support, community health workers or community paramedics, public health professionals, and interpreters as applicable, considering psychosocial needs and support resources.

source_anchor.table_row: People with social and/or structural barriers to care

canonical_statement: Table 1.1 recommends the following team-care approach for older adults: Use geriatric, pharmacy, diabetes education/nutrition, social services, case management, community services, and rehabilitation expertise as appropriate; assess nutrition, affordability/access, sensory, cognitive, dexterity, and mobility needs.

Table 1.1 recommends the following team-care approach for people in long-term care settings: Engage long-term-care clinicians, nurses, other health professionals, rehabilitation professionals, and nutrition professionals to ensure safe and appropriate diabetes management.

Table 1.1 recommends the following team-care approach for pregnant individuals with diabetes: Use pregnancy/diabetes expertise plus diabetes education, nutrition, eye care and other specialists as appropriate, with postpartum follow-up and transition back to established primary care.

Table 1.1 recommends the following team-care approach for people with behavioral health conditions: Engage behavioral health, care navigation, and social services as appropriate, using age- and situation-appropriate screening for general and diabetes-related psychosocial concerns.

The chapter concludes that improving health for people with and at risk for diabetes requires collaboration among individuals, health care systems, community resources, and broader social supports, with attention to quality, access, cost, and health disparities.
